1.translation: The Blessed Lord said: They speak of an imperishable aśvattha tree whose root is above and whose branches reach downward; its leaves are the Vedic hymns. Whoever knows this tree knows the Vedas.
1.nuances: All six agree on the inverted tree with Vedic hymns as leaves, but the tree is a peepul (Sivananda, Gambirananda), holy fig (Sankaranarayan), aśvattha left untranslated (Adidevananda) or a banyan (Prabhupāda). Purohit abandons the image almost entirely, paraphrasing it as phenomenal creation seeded in the Highest, while Sankaranarayan supplies the scriptures as the unnamed subject of prāhuḥ.

2.translation: Its branches, fed by the guṇas, spread downward and upward, and their shoots are the objects of the senses; below, in the world of human beings, further roots stretch out, bound to action.
2.nuances: The translators differ on guṇa (Sivananda and Purohit capitalise Qualities, Sankaranarayan uses Strands, Prabhupāda the three modes of material nature) and on whether the lower roots cause action (Sivananda), follow it (Gambirananda, Purohit) or bind to fruitive action (Prabhupāda). Gambirananda adds a gloss reading manuṣyaloke as the human body qualified by caste, and Adidevananda calls the lower roots secondary roots.

3.translation: Its form cannot be perceived here as it truly is, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation. Having felled this deep-rooted aśvattha with the firm axe of non-attachment,
3.nuances: Sampratiṣṭhā is rendered foundation or resting place (Sivananda), continuance (Gambirananda), support (Adidevananda), centre (Sankaranarayan) and strength (Purohit). Most render asaṅga-śastra as the axe of non-attachment; Gambirananda prefers sword and Prabhupāda the more general weapon, and Prabhupāda alone turns the participle into an injunction (one must cut).

4.translation: then one must search out that state from which, once reached, there is no return: I take refuge in that primal Person from whom the ancient stream of activity first flowed.
4.nuances: The sharpest split is over prapadye: Sivananda and Gambirananda keep the first person (I take refuge), Adidevananda and Prabhupāda convert it to an instruction to seek refuge or surrender, and Sankaranarayan reads it as the yogin attaining. Padam is goal, State, Path or Abode, and Prabhupāda expands the primal Person into the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

5.translation: Free of pride and delusion, having overcome the fault of attachment, ever fixed on the inner self, their desires wholly stilled, released from the pairs of opposites called pleasure and pain, the undeluded reach that imperishable state.
5.nuances: Gambirananda reads saṅga-doṣa as the evil of association with friends and foes and moha as non-discrimination, Adidevananda narrows moha to perverse notions about the self, and Prabhupāda renders māna as false prestige and adds surrender to the Supreme Person, which is absent in the Sanskrit. Adhyātma-nitya is variously dwelling in the Self, devoted to spirituality or understanding the eternal.

6.translation: Neither sun nor moon nor fire illuminates it; that is my supreme abode, from which those who reach it do not return.
6.nuances: Adidevananda, following Rāmānuja, reads taddhāma as the supreme light that is the individual self, while the others take it as Kṛṣṇa's abode. Prabhupāda adds electricity to the list of lights and specifies return to this material world, and Purohit inserts an address to Arjuna not present in the Sanskrit.

7.translation: A portion of my very self, having become the eternal living soul in the world of the living, draws to itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which rest in prakṛti.
7.nuances: Most read the eternal fragment as becoming the jīva and drawing the senses to itself; Adidevananda calls it the bound self and Sankaranarayan says it draws the senses into service. Prabhupāda pluralises into living entities who are struggling hard with the senses, a reading of karṣati not shared by the others, and Purohit stresses how very small the part is.

8.translation: When the lord of the body takes on a body and when he departs from it, he takes these senses and moves on, as the wind carries scents away from their source.
8.nuances: Īśvara is the crux: Sivananda glosses it as the individual soul, Gambirananda says master, Adidevananda Its lord, Sankaranarayan the Lord, and Purohit the Supreme Lord Himself. Prabhupāda replaces the senses with conceptions of life carried from body to body.

9.translation: Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste and smell, and over the mind, this soul enjoys the objects of the senses.
9.nuances: Sivananda, Gambirananda and Adidevananda keep the subject as the embodied self (it), Sankaranarayan and Purohit capitalise He, and Purohit goes furthest by making perception and enjoyment themselves divine. Prabhupāda reframes the verse as the acquisition of a new gross body.

10.translation: The deluded do not see the soul as it departs, stays, or experiences while joined to the guṇas; those with the eye of knowledge see it.
10.nuances: Guṇānvitam is attached by most to the departing soul, but Sankaranarayan attaches it to the object enjoyed and Purohit reads enjoyment through the Qualities. Sivananda, Purohit and Sankaranarayan refer to Him, Gambirananda and Adidevananda to it, and Prabhupāda recasts the verse around quitting the body under the modes of nature.

11.translation: Yogins who strive see this soul established within themselves; but those who have not disciplined themselves, lacking discernment, do not see it however hard they strive.
11.nuances: Akṛtātmānaḥ is rendered unrefined (Sivananda, Adidevananda), lacking self-control (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan), unable to control their minds (Purohit) and not situated in self-realization (Prabhupāda). Purohit calls the yogins saints, Prabhupāda transcendentalists.

12.translation: The radiance in the sun that lights the whole world, the radiance in the moon and in fire, know that radiance to be mine.
12.nuances: The translators essentially agree; the only variation is tejas as light, brilliance or splendor, Purohit's phrasing that the lights are born of Me, and Prabhupāda's addition that the sunlight dissipates darkness.

13.translation: Entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my vigour; becoming the sap-bearing soma, I nourish all plants.
13.nuances: Soma is the watery moon (Sivananda), cool moonbeams (Purohit), the sapful moon (Sankaranarayan), or kept as Soma with a note that most take it as the moon (Gambirananda, Adidevananda). Prabhupāda turns gām (earth) into each planet kept in orbit.

14.translation: Becoming the fire Vaiśvānara, I dwell in the bodies of living creatures and, joined with prāṇa and apāna, I digest the four kinds of food.
14.nuances: Vaiśvānara is kept as a name by Sivananda and Gambirananda and translated as the digestive fire or fire of life by the rest. Prāṇa and apāna are left untranslated or rendered as inward and outward breath, upward and downward winds, or outgoing and incoming air; Purohit loses the specific number four.

15.translation: I am seated in the heart of every being; from me come memory, knowledge and their loss. I alone am what is to be known through all the Vedas; I am the maker of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas.
15.nuances: Apohanam is read as loss or forgetfulness (Sivananda, Gambirananda, Prabhupāda), removal (Adidevananda) or, positively, discrimination and the faculty of differentiating (Purohit, Sankaranarayan). Vedānta-kṛt is the author or compiler of Vedānta for most, but Adidevananda reads it as the one who brings Vedic rituals to fruition, and Sankaranarayan adds that Kṛṣṇa authored the Vedas themselves.

16.translation: There are two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable: the perishable is all beings, and the one standing unchanging at the summit is called the imperishable.
16.nuances: Kūṭastha is the great divide: Gambirananda, following Śaṅkara, identifies the imperishable with māyā, Adidevananda keeps the two as kinds of Purusha with the unchanging liberated self, Sankaranarayan oddly gives spear-like One, and Prabhupāda reads fallible and infallible living entities in the material and spiritual worlds. Purohit reduces the persons to aspects in Nature.

17.translation: But the highest Person is another, called the supreme Self, the imperishable Lord who enters the three worlds and sustains them.
17.nuances: All agree on a third, supreme Person distinct from the two; Purohit alone turns it into first-person speech (higher than all am I). Adidevananda adds that the name is given in all the Vedas, and Prabhupāda calls Him the greatest living personality and Supreme Soul.

18.translation: Because I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama, the supreme Person.
18.nuances: Adidevananda reads loke as Smṛti rather than the world, giving a scripture pair. Purohit loosens the logic into being beyond comparison of eternal and non-eternal, and Prabhupāda renders kṣara and akṣara as fallible and infallible, consistent with his verse 16.

19.translation: Whoever, undeluded, knows me thus as the supreme Person knows everything, and worships me with his whole being, Bhārata.
19.nuances: Bhajati is worship for most, serve for Sankaranarayan and full devotional service for Prabhupāda. Purohit and Sivananda address Arjuna by name instead of Bhārata, and Prabhupāda replaces undeluded with without doubting.

20.translation: Thus I have taught this most secret teaching, sinless one; whoever understands it becomes wise and has fulfilled all that must be done, Bhārata.
20.nuances: Śāstra is science (Sivananda), scripture (Gambirananda, Sankaranarayan), doctrine (Adidevananda), mystic knowledge (Purohit) or the most confidential part of the Vedic scriptures (Prabhupāda). Kṛtakṛtya ranges from duties accomplished to the consummation of life (Purohit) and endeavors knowing perfection (Prabhupāda).

21.translation: Oṁ, That is the Real. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, called the Yoga of the Supreme Person, in the Upaniṣads of the glorious Bhagavad Gītā, the knowledge of Brahman, the scripture of yoga, the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
